significance.justification: Verified true, the claim would establish that multilingual refusal follows a form-(iii) predictive coupling—"systematically lower refusal activation in low-resource languages" produces higher jailbreak success through a shared direction—plus a form-(ii) causal result in which threshold equalization restores refusal. This fixes expected orderings across languages and links the behavioral phenomenon documented by Yong et al., "Low-Resource Languages Jailbreak GPT-4" (ICLR 2024), to the kind of residual-stream mechanism studied by Arditi et al., "Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction" (NeurIPS 2024), thereby providing both a weighty phenomenon and a causal mechanism rather than merely another representation probe. Refutation would meaningfully rule out a shared one-dimensional threshold account of the multilingual safety gap, although the wording is only partly determinate because "the effective activation threshold...is...lower" is said both to prevent prompts from crossing it and to be repaired by "lowering the threshold," which are opposite threshold semantics. After topic substitution, the generic question of shared versus language-specific multilingual mechanisms would not retain this score; the specific activation-resource-vulnerability coupling and causal equalization are what place it above the topic-median hypothesis.

reach.justification: The named handles are "per-language refusal-trigger thresholds" as a diagnostic and the interventions "adding the shared refusal direction" or "equalize threshold" as deployment controls. The diagnostic is mainly post hoc as written—activation is related to observed "jailbreak success" and "known low-resource jailbreaks"—but the intervention could be used by model auditors or deployers, not only by researchers analyzing the mechanism. After per-model re-extraction, the claim predicts a transferable ordering and coupling—low-resource languages should have lower refusal activation and sub-threshold activation should forecast vulnerability—although it does not specify transferable numerical thresholds or explicit scope across architectures, scales, and training regimes. The topic-substitution check lowers the reach attributable merely to multilingual safety; the score is supported instead by the concrete audit quantity, practitioner-facing control, and cross-language relation asserted by this claim.
